cases.name: abbreviation: Dr. Reyes
cases.note: A stop after a listed abbreviation (Dr) does not end the sentence.

content.text: Dr. Reyes signed the letter. She posted it at noon.

cases.text: Dr. Reyes signed the letter. She posted it at noon.

passages.text: Dr. Reyes signed the letter. She posted it at noon.

cases.name: abbreviations and times
cases.note: Mr is listed; dotted letters (p.m.) before a lower-case word do not end a sentence.

content.text: Mr. Smith went to Washington. He arrived at 5 p.m. on Monday.

cases.text: Mr. Smith went to Washington. He arrived at 5 p.m. on Monday.

sentences.text: He arrived at 5 p.m. on Monday.

passages.text: He arrived at 5 p.m. on Monday.
Mr. Smith went to Washington. He arrived at 5 p.m. on Monday.

cases.name: quoted speech ending a sentence
cases.note: Closing quotes after the stop stay with their sentence; the next sentence starts after the space.

content.text: She said, "We leave at dawn." The others nodded.

cases.text: She said, "We leave at dawn." The others nodded.

passages.text: She said, "We leave at dawn." The others nodded.

cases.name: closing quotes after the stop
cases.note: Same rule with no comma before the quote.
cases.text: He said "Stop." Then he left!

cases.name: quoted speech inside a sentence
cases.note: A lower-case word after the closing quote continues the sentence.
cases.text: "Stop!" she said. Nobody moved.

cases.name: ellipsis, question, emoji
cases.note: An ellipsis before a lower-case word continues; ? and ! end; an emoji may open the next sentence.

content.text: Is it? Yes... it is. Great day! 🎉 Next one.

cases.text: Is it? Yes... it is. Great day! 🎉 Next one.

cases.name: ellipsis before a capital
cases.note: An ellipsis before a capital ends the sentence. Knowingly crude: a name after an ellipsis also ends it.
cases.text: He waited... Then he left.

cases.name: initials and dotted abbreviations
cases.note: A one-letter word before a stop is an initial. Dotted letters (U.S.) end a sentence when a capital follows, so "The U.S. Army" splits: knowingly crude.

content.text: J. R. R. Tolkien wrote it. The U.S. Army read it.

cases.text: J. R. R. Tolkien wrote it. The U.S. Army read it.

sentences.text: J. R. R. Tolkien wrote it.

passages.text: J. R. R. Tolkien wrote it.
J. R. R. Tolkien wrote it. The U.S.

cases.name: crude: one capital letter before a stop
cases.note: Knowingly crude: "B." is read as an initial, so this is one sentence.

content.text: We chose plan B. Then we left.

cases.text: We chose plan B. Then we left.

sentences.text: We chose plan B. Then we left.

passages.text: We chose plan B. Then we left.

cases.name: crude: a sentence that starts in lower case
cases.note: Knowingly crude: a stop before a lower-case word never ends a sentence, so this is one sentence.

content.text: Sales rose in March. eBay fell later.

cases.text: Sales rose in March. eBay fell later.

sentences.text: Sales rose in March. eBay fell later.

passages.text: Sales rose in March. eBay fell later.

cases.name: list number and e.g.
cases.note: A number that opens a sentence keeps its stop; e.g is listed.

content.text: 1. First item is here. Second, e.g. this one.

cases.text: 1. First item is here. Second, e.g. this one.

passages.text: 1. First item is here. Second, e.g. this one.

cases.name: decimals and versions
cases.note: A stop with no space after it (3.14) never ends a sentence.
cases.text: Pi is 3.14 today. Version 2.0 ships.

cases.name: no terminator
cases.note: A block without a stop is one sentence that runs to the block end.
cases.text: No terminator at the end

cases.name: curly quotes and apostrophes
cases.note: Curly quotes are closers like straight ones.
cases.text: “It’s late.” She left. ‘Fine,’ he said.

cases.name: whitespace runs and a newline
cases.note: Sentence text keeps the article's own spacing; the id normalises every whitespace run to one space.

content.text:
First  sentence
wraps here. Second one.

cases.text:
First  sentence
wraps here. Second one.

passages.text:
First  sentence
wraps here. Second one.

cases.name: a sentence across inline marks and a link
cases.note: A sentence may span several text nodes; marks and links change neither offsets nor text.

content.text: . It is wrong by four minutes.

cases.text: Read the timetable twice. It is wrong by four minutes.

sentences.text: It is wrong by four minutes.

passages.text: It is wrong by four minutes.
Read the timetable twice. It is wrong by four minutes.

cases.name: headings
cases.note: A heading is a block: its own sentence without a stop; a stop inside it splits as in a paragraph.
cases.text: Morning crossingPart two. The returnText follows.

cases.name: list items
cases.note: Each list item is a block; sentences never join across items.
cases.text: Tickets at the pierCoffee on board. Tea too.Arrive early.

passages.text: Tickets at the pier Coffee on board.

cases.name: blocks, marks, hard break and a list
cases.note: A hard break counts as whitespace after a stop; a blockquote holds ordinary paragraph blocks.
cases.text: A heading without a stopBold words end here. Then more.Line one.Line two.Item one. Item two.Quoted line.

passages.text: A heading without a stop Bold words end here.

cases.name: full-width terminators
cases.note: Full-width 。！？ end a sentence with no space after them.

content.text: 这是第一句。这是第二句！

cases.text: 这是第一句。这是第二句！

passages.text: 这是第一句。这是第二句！

cases.name: Japanese without a final stop
cases.note: The last sentence has no stop and runs to the block end.

content.text: 今日は晴れです。明日は雨

cases.text: 今日は晴れです。明日は雨

passages.text: 今日は晴れです。明日は雨

cases.name: Thai, no sentence punctuation
cases.note: Knowingly crude: Thai separates sentences with spaces, not punctuation, so the whole block is one sentence.

content.text: วันนี้อากาศดี เราไปทะเลกัน

cases.text: วันนี้อากาศดี เราไปทะเลกัน

sentences.text: วันนี้อากาศดี เราไปทะเลกัน

passages.text: วันนี้อากาศดี เราไปทะเลกัน

cases.name: Hindi with the danda
cases.note: The danda (U+0964) ends a sentence like a full stop.

content.text: मैं घर जा रहा हूँ। तुम कहाँ हो?

cases.text: मैं घर जा रहा हूँ। तुम कहाँ हो?

passages.text: मैं घर जा रहा हूँ। तुम कहाँ हो?

cases.name: Hebrew, right to left
cases.note: Right-to-left text is handled in logical (stored) order; a script without case never meets the lower-case rule.
cases.text: שלום לכולם. מה שלומכם היום?

cases.name: Arabic, right to left
cases.note: The Arabic question mark (U+061F) ends a sentence.
cases.text: كيف حالك؟ أنا بخير.

cases.name: emoji sequences
cases.note: Emoji, skin tones and joiners are ordinary characters; offsets count UTF-16 code units.
cases.text: Well done 👍🏽. The team 👩‍👩‍👧 cheered!

cases.name: no as a word ends a sentence
cases.note: "no." keeps a sentence open only before a number.

content.text: The answer was no. She left anyway.

cases.text: The answer was no. She left anyway.

passages.text: The answer was no. She left anyway.

cases.name: no. before a number
cases.note: "no." before a digit is an abbreviation.

content.text: See no. 5 on the list. Then go.

cases.text: See no. 5 on the list. Then go.

passages.text: See no. 5 on the list. Then go.

cases.name: fig as a word and before a number
cases.note: "fig." keeps a sentence open only before a number.

content.text: She ate a fig. It was ripe. See fig. 3 for more.

cases.text: She ate a fig. It was ripe. See fig. 3 for more.

passages.text: She ate a fig. It was ripe.

cases.name: p.m. before a capital
cases.note: Dotted letters end a sentence when a capital follows.

content.text: We met at 5 p.m. She was late.

cases.text: We met at 5 p.m. She was late.

passages.text: We met at 5 p.m. She was late.

cases.name: U.S. before a capital
cases.note: Dotted letters end a sentence when a capital follows.

content.text: He lives in the U.S. The weather is fine.

cases.text: He lives in the U.S. The weather is fine.

passages.text: He lives in the U.S. The weather is fine.

cases.name: a punctuation-only run joins the sentence before it
cases.note: A piece with no letter or digit is not a sentence of its own.
cases.text: Wait . . . ? ! Then go.

cases.name: a block of punctuation only
cases.note: A block with no letter or digit at all is one sentence.

cases.name: an emoji-only paragraph
cases.note: A block with no letter or digit is still one sentence, so it can be tipped.

cases.name: Armenian full stop
cases.note: The Armenian full stop (U+0589) ends a sentence when a space follows.
cases.text: Բարեւ։ Ինչպես ես։

cases.name: full-width and half-width stops
cases.note: U+FF0E and U+FF61 end a sentence with no space after them.
cases.text: 一つ．二つ｡三つ

cases.name: Greek question mark
cases.note: The Greek question mark (U+037E) ends a sentence; the id uses NFC, which maps it to U+003B.
cases.text: Τι κάνεις; Καλά.

cases.name: a hard break reads as a space
cases.note: A hard break inside a sentence gives one space in its text; offsets count no character for it.
cases.text: Roses are red,violets are blue.

sentences.text: Roses are red, violets are blue.

passages.text: Roses are red, violets are blue.

cases.name: U+0085 is not whitespace
cases.note: NEL (U+0085) is kept as a character, never read as a space.
cases.text: Lineone ends. Two.

cases.name: U+200B is not whitespace
cases.note: ZERO WIDTH SPACE (U+200B) is kept as a character, never read as a space.
cases.text: Zero​width here. Next.

cases.name: decomposed accent (NFC in the id)
cases.note: Text kept as stored; the id uses NFC, so it equals the precomposed case.
cases.text: Café au lait. Done.

cases.name: precomposed accent (NFC in the id)
cases.note: Same id as the decomposed case.
cases.text: Café au lait. Done.

cases.name: straight apostrophe
cases.note: Quotes are kept as written: this id differs from the curly apostrophe case.
cases.text: It's late. Go.

cases.name: curly apostrophe
cases.note: Differs from the straight apostrophe case.
cases.text: It’s late. Go.
